runtime_cross_checks.evidence: In the AI-owned control, descriptor index 1 populated combatant record 1 and resolved to participant index 0, the player contesting participant 1's Gate. This matches the static rule that record 1 is the active or thrown challenger.

The player-owned control records participant 1 contesting participant 0's Gate with the same session descriptor pair ordering. The identity-agnostic collision code places the active descriptor in +0x28E regardless of which participant is human or owns the Gate.

player_ai_behavior: The collision and descriptor-pair code is participant-identity agnostic. Human/AI status does not alter target-first and active-second ordering. The authoritative human/AI source remains reserved for checkpoint 2D.
scripted_behavior: All seven direct overlay-7 calls to the pair setter preserve active descriptor in r2/+0x28E. Two paths use the same active descriptor for both arguments when no distinct target exists. When +0x28D equals +0x28E, the context has no distinct defender/challenger pair and System 2.0 must not infer an opponent relation from record index alone.
supported_conclusions: For a distinct two-combatant collision, combatant record 0 is the stationary target or defender and combatant record 1 is the active or thrown challenger.
The canonical challenging descriptor is session +0x28E, not a Gate-owner-relative or human-relative field.
The canonical challenging participant is the low nibble of descriptor byte +0x0F for the descriptor selected by session +0x28E.
Gate owner and challenger are independent identities: the owner remains battle object +0x06, while the challenger derives from the active descriptor.
The ordering rule is shared across player and AI actions because no audited call site branches on human/AI identity when assigning the pair.
Equal descriptor indices represent a no-distinct-target fallback and must not be interpreted as a normal challenge.
